An underdog is a person, team, animal, or group that is widely expected to lose, fail, or be defeated — especially when compared to a stronger, more powerful, or more favored opponent.

Think of it simply as: the one nobody believes in.

The word captures two important things at once:

1. A position of weakness or disadvantage.
The underdog is not just losing — they are in a situation where the odds are stacked against them. They have less power, less resources, less skill, less support, or less experience than their opponent or competition.

2. An expectation of failure.
The underdog is the one that most people — experts, observers, the public — predict will not succeed. This is crucial. It is not just about being weak; it is about being counted out by others.

So an underdog is not simply someone who is struggling. They are someone who is struggling and whom the world has largely given up on.

"Underdog" appears in many areas of life:

In sports: When a small, unknown team plays against a powerful, celebrated champion, the small team is the underdog. Everyone expects the champion to win easily.

In competitions and contests: A new singer competing against established stars is an underdog. A young, inexperienced politician running against a powerful, well-funded veteran is an underdog.

In business: A tiny startup trying to compete with a giant, billion-dollar company is an underdog. Almost nobody expects it to survive, let alone succeed.

In life and society: A person from a poor background trying to get into a top university, or someone with no connections trying to break into a highly competitive industry — they are underdogs. The system, the circumstances, and the statistics are all working against them.

"Underdog" is not a neutral, cold word. It carries a strong emotional charge, and that emotion is almost always one of sympathy and admiration.

When people hear that someone is an underdog, they naturally feel for them. There is something deeply human about rooting for the one who has been overlooked, dismissed, or underestimated. It touches on values like fairness, hope, and the belief that hard work and determination can overcome a lack of resources or privilege.

This is why the phrase "rooting for the underdog" is so common. People cheer for the underdog not because they think they will win, but because most others think they won't.
The Underdog Can Win — and That's the Point

Here is the most exciting and important thing about underdogs: they sometimes do win. And when they do, it feels extraordinary.

If the favorite wins, people simply nod — it was expected. But if the underdog wins, it is called an upset, and it becomes a story people tell for years. This is because the underdog's victory defies expectations, and that is rare and thrilling.

The possibility — however slim — that the underdog could succeed is what makes the concept so compelling. If an underdog had zero chance of winning, there would be no story. It is the against-the-odds possibility of success that defines them.

The opposite of an underdog is the favorite (also called the frontrunner). The favorite is the one expected to win — the stronger, more powerful, more experienced side. Where the underdog has little support and low expectations, the favorite has confidence, resources, and the crowd's prediction behind them.

The underdog label is relative. Someone can be an underdog in one situation but not in another. A regional chess champion is an underdog at a national tournament but a favorite at a local school event.

Being called an underdog is sometimes used as motivation. Athletes, politicians, and business leaders sometimes embrace the underdog label on purpose — because being underestimated can fuel a stronger effort and remove pressure. "No one believes in us" can be a battle cry.

You can be your own underdog. The word is sometimes used to describe someone who has had to fight against their own life circumstances — poverty, illness, discrimination — not just a single opponent. In this sense, the "opponent" is life itself.

The underdog is not necessarily bad or inferior in character. They may simply lack advantages. Many underdogs are highly talented, hard-working, and admirable — they just lack the resources, connections, reputation, or luck that their opponents have.

• "Nobody gave them a chance, but the underdog team won the championship."
  • "She was the underdog in the race — no money, no name recognition — but she won anyway."
  • "I've always been an underdog, and that's why I work twice as hard as everyone else."
  • "The whole country was rooting for the underdog."
  • "Don't underestimate him — underdogs have a habit of surprising people."

If you had to capture the entire word in a single sentence:

An underdog is someone who is at a disadvantage and expected to fail — but who carries the inspiring possibility of proving everyone wrong.
